newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary's trade gap lower than foreseen - ministry. [CORRECTED 11:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Hungary's trade gap lower than foreseen - ministry. [CORRECTED 11:40 GMT]

text.p: Hungary's trade deficit is lower than expected, and the preliminary January-March figure is likely to be revised substantially downwards later, the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Tourism (MIT) said on Friday.
The ministry said earlier on Friday that according to preliminary figures, the trade gap was $690 million in the first quarter of the year, up from $431.4 million in the January-February period.

But MIT Deputy Secretary of State Lajos Berenyi told a news conference that belated figures of lease work exports and duty-free zones were likely to boost the final January-March exports figure by at least $150 million.
"According to last year's experience... final export figures will be at least $150 million higher," he said.
"There may be additions to the imports data but the extent of these will be much smaller."
Berenyi said the final January-February trade gap figures showed a reduction of some $186 million from the preliminary $431.4 million (Corrects to delete reference to import and export figures).
The ministry said that it would publish final detailed January-February trade deficit figures later on Friday.
Berenyi said finalised trade data showed higher exports than foreseen, while imports rose at the expected pace.

He added that the first quarter figures clearly indicated that economic growth had started in the country, which posted gross domestic product (GDP) growth of some one percent last year and plans about three percent for 1997.

"Industrial production (in Q1) increased by some six percent according to the preliminary figures, while exports are by eight to nine percent higher than in the same period of 1996," he said, adding that imports rose by nine to 10 percent.
However, he added that that the final figures were likely to show exports rose more rapidly than imports.
Berenyi said the most dynamically growing industrial sector in exports was the machinery industry which accounted for some 39 percent of all exports.
He added that a developed country can be satisfied with that rate but the weight of lease work in Hungary's exports -- some 25 percent -- was larger than in developed countries.

The volume of Hungary's retail trade dropped by 12 percent in the first two months of 1997, the MIT said in a statement, but Berenyi added that according to a fresh survey of the think-tank Kopint-Datorg retail trade volume rose substantially in March.
"I am convinced that retail trade turnover will grow this year," he said, adding that real wages increased by five to six percent in the first quarter, while household savings stagnated.

Berenyi said the ministry maintained its forecast for a trade deficit of around $3 billion for this year, and the government was looking at opportunities to reduce the forint's monthly 1.2 percent devaluation rate after June.
Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy told Reuters earlier this week that there was a good chance for the trade deficit to remain below $3 billion this year.
